connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
duration: for about 7 years, since I immigrated
disclosure_text: As an immigrant from the middle east, I sometimes feel out of place in my home, Canada. Not because I'm not familiar with the culture but because I'm not sure how I'm viewed by "Canadians".
micronarrative:
What I find quite interesting is that the real experience is being lost in chaos, and this is what I have experienced with my flesh and bone. No one wants to hear from the ones who have lived in experience and rather stick to a familiar narrative. Being from Iran and having lived there for 30+ years, and having experienced the brutalities in every aspect of my life means so little to a considerable population here in the west. They think they know the truth but they don't; they're just louder and have more platform.

When I speak to colleagues about how dangerous the government is, they don't believe me and instead ask how sure I am of these so-called dangers. They think we Iranians are making up stories because the oppression is too much for their understanding. My colleague and I were talking about how Iran has always chanted death to America, and my colleague asked me with a high-pitched voice: "Do they mean it though?" It made my blood boil. I just smiled and changed the subject.

I just wanted to stop talking with her about this because I was tired of trying to prove the truth. I said something along the lines of "how politicians are playing with the masses" and moved on. The frustration and the feeling of being dismissed are so overwhelming, but I know that my voice matters, and I will continue to share my experiences whenever I can.

annotations.tweet_text: I believe women. I also believe due process. These shouldn't be mutually exclusive.
annotations.participant_label: Likely not harmful — critical or provocative, but the harm reading requires a stretch
annotations.rationale: My initial thought was that this post is related to the Me Too movement and more specifically to those taking advantage of this movement for their personal gain by targeting people who were actually innocent. I do like that it is highlighting due process making sure justice is served regardless off the issue.

annotations.tweet_text: Calling everything a 'microaggression' doesn't empower women. It treats them like they can't handle everyday life.
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful — policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.rationale: I believe this post is nothing but an observation. Not every little comment is necessarily a micro aggression. I think, being a woman myself, focusing too much on what people say to us or how treat us and connecting it to our gender makes us mentally weaker and more fragile.

annotations.tweet_text: There are two genders. I'm sorry if that's hurtful, but being hurtful isn't the same as being wrong.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous — could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: A very controversial comment which can provoke some groups. It offers a binary view on gender and highlights that truth should be judged because it causes discomfort. I think this comment also reflects a disagreement about gender is defined and who gets to define it and leaves out those who claim not to fit in either group.

annotations.tweet_text: If gender is a social construct, then so is the wage gap. You can't have it both ways.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful — framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.rationale: The writer of this comment is accusing someone of being inconsistent and is trying to catch someone in their act. The comment however is a bit confusing to me. Not every inequality is explained in the same way. Wage gap has multiple causes not just social and this is oversimplifying the issue.

annotations.tweet_text: Women's sports existed to give women a fair playing field. That's it. That's the whole point.
annotations.participant_label: Likely not harmful — critical or provocative, but the harm reading requires a stretch
annotations.rationale: I am quite certain that this post is targeted at trans women in sports and how their presence can throw off the fairness of the game as they are biologically male and therefore are stronger and can perform better that females. The comment is stating a clear fact but it will still provoke certain groups.

annotations.tweet_text: Men aren't broken women. Treating masculinity as a pathology isn't progressivism, it's prejudice with better vocabulary.
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful — policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.rationale: This comment is simply saying that women are not the "standard" human and men are not defective in any way. It's pushing back against the idea that masculinity is wrong or unhealthy. It also suggests that calling masculinity toxic or problematic is not a progressive way of thinking but it is a form of prejudice or bias.

annotations.tweet_text: When a working-class white man loses a job to a diversity hire, he's not allowed to be angry. That anger has to go somewhere.

annotations.rationale: I can sense frustration and disappointment in this comment. It is clear that white men specifically are being targeted in this modern age under the label of promoting diversity. It suggest that employers are not hiring based on merit but based on the popular narrative of "diverse work environment" which has left some groups like white men out.

annotations.tweet_text: Intersectionality is just a hierarchy that puts some victims above others. It's oppression with extra steps.
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful — policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.rationale: I believe this comment is highlighting how society has been picking and choosing who deserves more pity. It creates a ranking of who is more oppressed which makes everything more complicated and unfair. I think the writer maybe talking about a ranking system of victimhood in which people decide who is more important and/or more oppressed than others.

annotations.tweet_text: First-generation immigrant women are often the most opposed to feminism. Nobody ever asks them why.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous — could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why

annotations.tweet_text: We have a word for communities where women can't leave the house without permission. We're just not allowed to use it anymore.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous — could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: I believe this comment is talking about restrictions on women and how patriarchy is in the core of it. The comment is hinting at the fact that using the correct label for this concept can have consequences. The sentence is somewhat vague and can be dragged to different discussions but it is clearly targeting communities in which women are in some way limited.

reflexivity_response: I believe that being a woman, being an immigrant, being from a middle eastern country where I have experienced oppression not just as a woman but as someone with different values, I can understand injustice when I see it. Looking back at my responses, I think I have tried to consider if the writer was trying to be provocative or speak their truth.
